\chapter{Hic, Iste, Ille, Is, Ibi}
\label{ch:la-demonstrativa}
\hlchaptermodality{50}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something near me, something near you and something over there, refer back to a person already named, and say that a thing is there.}

The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hic, haec, hoc]{hic — the near point of a three-way system Spanish still keeps}

\label{lesson:LA-C50-hic}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quandō} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{possum} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lūx} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{veniō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pluit} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ūndecim — vīgintī} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hic, haec, hoc} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{this},\textquotedblright{} the one near me.

Latin points three ways, and this is the first of the three. \textbf{Hic} is the thing in the speaker's own hand or reach.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Hic liber.} — This book (here, mine).
\end{quote}

Three forms because it agrees with its noun: \textbf{hic} for a masculine one, \textbf{haec} for a feminine one, \textbf{hoc} for a neuter one — the same three-way agreement \emph{quī} showed you last chapter.

The system survived. Spanish still points three ways — \emph{este}, \emph{ese}, \emph{aquel} — and it is Latin's system, arriving through a different set of words. Italian, French and Portuguese all collapsed to two. So a Spanish speaker meeting \emph{hic, iste, ille} is meeting the shape of their own grammar in its original three pieces.

English \textbf{ad hoc} is \emph{hoc}, \textquotedblleft{}for this\textquotedblright{}; a \textbf{hic jacet} is what an old gravestone says: \textquotedblleft{}here lies.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hic, haec, hoc}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many ways does Latin point? (\textbf{Three}.) Which one is \emph{hic}? (\textbf{The one near me}.) Which modern language kept all three? (\textbf{Spanish}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[iste, ista, istud]{iste — the middle point, and the one Latin used to sneer with}

\label{lesson:LA-C50-iste}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hic} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{volō} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{umbra} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dīcō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pluit} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ūndecim — vīgintī} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{iste, ista, istud} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{that},\textquotedblright{} the one near \textbf{you}.

The middle term, and the one with an attitude. \emph{Iste} is literally \textquotedblleft{}that of yours,\textquotedblright{} and Roman orators used it to keep a thing at arm's length. Cicero's speeches are full of \textbf{iste} meaning \textquotedblleft{}that man of yours\textquotedblright{} with a curl of the lip — the word does the sneering, and no adjective is needed.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Iste liber.} — That book of yours.
\end{quote}

Then the words moved. Spanish \textbf{este} (\textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{}) is from \emph{iste}, not from \emph{hic} — the middle term slid down into the near slot when \emph{hic} dropped out, and \emph{ipse} slid in behind it to make \emph{ese}. So Spanish still points three ways and does it with a different three words, which is a good demonstration that a SYSTEM can outlive every word in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{iste, ista, istud}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is \emph{iste}? (\textbf{Near you}.) What tone can it carry? (\textbf{Contempt} — Cicero's \textquotedblleft{}that man of yours\textquotedblright{}.) Which Spanish word came from it? (\emph{\textbf{Este}} — and it moved slot.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ille, illa, illud]{ille — the far point, and the word that became the Romance article}

\label{lesson:LA-C50-ille}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{iste} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quī} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{stēlla} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dīcō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ūndecim — vīgintī} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{canis} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ille, illa, illud} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{that},\textquotedblright{} the one over \textbf{there}, away from both of us.

The far term, and the most consequential word in this chapter — because it did not stay a demonstrative.

Latin had \textbf{no article} (this book's inventory records that as a demand it never states). Vulgar Latin invented one, and it invented it out of \emph{ille}. Say \emph{ille} often enough and unstressed, in front of a noun, and it wears down:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{wore down to} \\
\midrule
\emph{ille} & Italian \textbf{il}, French \textbf{le}, Spanish \textbf{el} \\
\emph{illa} & Italian and Spanish \textbf{la}, French \textbf{la} \\
\emph{illī} & Spanish \textbf{ellos}, French \textbf{ils} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The same word became the definite article \textbf{and} the third-person pronoun in every Romance language. Your very first lesson taught you that Latin's endings carry what other languages carry in extra words; here is the reverse motion, a demonstrative flattening into an extra word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ille, illa, illud}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is \emph{ille}? (\textbf{Over there}, away from both.) What did it become? (\textbf{The definite article and the third-person pronoun} of every Romance language.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[is, ea, id]{is — the pronoun Latin does not really have, doing the job anyway}

\label{lesson:LA-C50-is}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ille} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{et} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lūna} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{videō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ūndecim — vīgintī} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{canis} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{is, ea, id} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he, she, it}.\textquotedblright{}

Latin has \textbf{no dedicated third-person pronoun}. What it has is \emph{is, ea, id} — a demonstrative with no deixis left in it, neither near nor far, pressed into the job. \emph{Hic} points at something; \emph{is} merely refers back to something already named.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Amīcus venit. Is bene valet.} — A friend is coming. He is well.
\end{quote}

Its neuter, \textbf{id}, is a word English took whole: Freud's \emph{das Es} was rendered into English as the \textbf{id}, Latin for \textquotedblleft{}it.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Identical} and \textbf{identity} are \emph{idem}, \textquotedblleft{}the same one.\textquotedblright{} And an \textbf{idiom} is not from this at all — that is Greek \emph{idios}, \textquotedblleft{}one's own,\textquotedblright{} and the resemblance is a coincidence.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{is, ea, id}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Latin have a real third-person pronoun? (\textbf{No} — \emph{is, ea, id} does the job.) Where does Freud's \emph{id} come from? (\textbf{Latin \emph{id}}, \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ibi]{ibi — the place word the corpus has gone fifty chapters without}

\label{lesson:LA-C50-ibi}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{is} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quandō} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{somnus} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{videō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{canis} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{viridis} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ibi} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{there}.\textquotedblright{}

Every demonstrative in this chapter has an adverb beside it, and this is the pair that matters most: \textbf{hīc} (\textquotedblleft{}here\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{ibi} (\textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Liber hīc est. Amīcus ibi est.} — The book is here. The friend is there.
\end{quote}

Note the macron. The pronoun is \textbf{hic}, short; the adverb \textquotedblleft{}here\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{hīc}, long. Same four letters, different words, and only the vowel length tells them apart — which is the whole argument for writing macrons, made once more.

\emph{Ibi} survives into Italian \emph{ivi} and, worn down almost to nothing, into the French \textbf{y} of \emph{il y a} — \textquotedblleft{}there is.\textquotedblright{} A single letter of modern French is this Latin word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the book is here\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}the friend is there.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Liber hīc est. Amīcus ibi est}}.) What separates the pronoun \emph{hic} from the adverb \emph{hīc}? (\textbf{Vowel length} — the macron.)
\end{tcolorbox}
